There's two weird things (arguably, bugs) that happen with this code. Points if you can predict the messages produced by this without running it!

axiom RiemannHypothesis : Prop

theorem foo (h : RiemannHypothesis) (f : Nat → Nat) : RiemannHypothesis := by
  simpa? [*] using f "Hello world!"

Spoiler

1) Even though f "Hello world!" is not well-formed, simpa resolves the goal before ever trying to elaborate the using .... part, so it never gives an error. A minimal example is

example : True := by
  simpa using g

which works fine even though there's no g in context.

2) The simpa? message is nonsense and suggests simpa only using f "Hello world!", which of course doesn't work. It should be one of simp [h], simp [*], or simp only [h] or simp only [*]. (I think the correct answer is simp only [h].) I'm guessing this is somehow related to some bug where the simpa? version tried to elaborate the conclusion and failed and this caused something else to go astray.
What is the preferred behaviour here? It would be great if we could get simpa fixed, but I don't have the time right now to try writing a spec for it.
I'm happy to "make it so" if there's agreement on what changes we want.

The (1) part seems not too important, arguably the ideal behavior right now. It already prints a warning if the concluding term isn't used, which seems like the best behavior (no need to try to throw an error if we have a working proof.)

But for (2), the suggested message is wrong, and I think that should be fixed. I thought the buggy behavior was exactly:

  • You call simpa? [hypot] using term and term has an error. It incorrectly thinks that hypot isn't used, and suggests simpa only using term, which doesn't work.

But that isn't true, because this also fails:

theorem foo : ∀ (x : Nat), x + 0 = 0 + x := by
  simpa? --Try this:  [apply] simpa only

where the suggestion of course also doesn't work.

In this case, simp can close the goal using three lemmas from core, but for some reason simpa? doesn't suggest using any of them. It seems like this only happens when simpa? doesn't end up actually needing an assumption. It just skips outputting any lemmas at all!

The return {} here is incorrect, and it should be returning stats. That's the reason for the simpa? issue.

That same bit of code is responsible for the linter warning you get for a simpa that could be a simp. I'm leaning toward it being an actual error if there's an unnecessary using clause.

Please don't make it an error!
I know people writing simp calls by throwing in stuff until it works and then removing unused arga when it works
It would also be very inconsistent for simpa to throw an error and for simp not to

Moritz Roos said:

It would also be very inconsistent for simpa to throw an error and for simp not to

I think this is only about bad using clauses being an error, which simp doesn't have. This isn't about the simplification lemma list, in []
I think it's in the same spirit as the simp lemma list
I also don't really see any advantages of it being an error rather than a warning
Also I remember faintly some plan to implement simpa with some simp call(s) in the future which maybe? would clash with this?

@Moritz Roos With simpa [args...] using e, the experience currently is that you get errors if any of the args are malformed. Then once you get those right, either

  1. simp [args...] closes the goal immediately on its own. In that case, it currently gives a linter warning that simpa could be simp. It completely ignores e`, and it could be a bunch of nonsense.
  2. simp [args...] doesn't close the goal. Then, effectively, have tmp := e is elaborated, then simp [args...] at tmp is applied, and finally it does exact e. It gives an error unless exact e works.

So, you get errors throughout the process already, in a reasonably natural way. Conceptually simpa [args...] using e is have tmp := e; simp [args...] at tmp |-; exact tmp, so it's weird if exact tmp isn't giving an error. The current implementation is as if it's simp [args...] at tmp |- <;> exact tmp, which I don't think is expected.

If there were a simp% term elaborator, I imagine that you are thinking of simpa [args...] using e to be like simp [args..., simp% e]. I agree that it shouldn't be an error to have an unused simp argument. However, with simpa, it's currently inconsistent among the tactics as being one that only conditionally elaborates one of its arguments.
Basically, simpa ... using is a way to get around the usual "no nonterminal simps" prohibition. I myself see it as the "simp_exact" tactic.

Kyle Miller schrieb:

I'm leaning toward it being an actual error if there's an unnecessary using clause.

did you mean to write malformed using clause here?

I mean unnecessary, in the sense that "the errors of simpa should coincide with the errors you get in have tmp := e; simp [args...] at tmp |-; exact tmp". An unnecessary using clause corresponds to exact failing due to "no goals to be solved".
This is the change how i hope simpa will be changed to
i really don't think of it using exact, even if that is basically the current implementation

I see simpa [args...] as simp [args]; assumption (that's the "a"), and using is meant to override which assumption you use. It's possibly an abuse of simpa that you can give the using clause an arbitrary term, rather than a single hypothesis.
I find this much to unflexible of an implementation :)
What do you think about simp itself having a using clause, and the way simp [args...] using [args...] worked is the way you expect it to?

Kyle Miller said:

It's possibly an abuse of simpa that you can give the using clause an arbitrary term, rather than a single hypothesis.

the only alternative I can see is have := arbitrary_term; simpa [...] which imo looks much worse

Right, that's why simpa is relaxed @Aaron Liu. The broader context is that I'm wondering if it would be best to deprecate complex terms for using on simpa itself, and have a separate simp_exact tactic.

Kyle Miller schrieb:

What do you think about simp itself having a using clause, and the way simp [args...] using [args...] worked is the way you expect it to?

I would then vote for abolishing the current simpa, since i don't think it's ever a good idea to call assumption after a simp
See Floris arguments on why changing the semantics is a good idea
Why should i use the implementation with exact, if we also have the more flexible implementation that will not break as easily under new simp lemmas?
Thanks for the pointer @Moritz Roos. I've continued discussion at #mathlib4 > Mathlib code quality: simpa @ 💬
